paper.title_en: Charge Exchange Illuminates Turbulent Cold-Hot Interfaces
paper.abstract_en: Cold-hot interfaces are ubiquitous in the multiphase circumgalactic medium (CGM), galactic winds, and the Galactic Center (GC), yet their microscopic contact regions are difficult to observe. Charge exchange (CX), in which a highly ionized metal ion captures an electron from a neutral donor and emits soft X-ray lines, directly probes these interfaces. We develop a subgrid CX model coupled to a nonequilibrium ionization (NEI) network in hydrodynamic simulations of radiative turbulent mixing layers. CX soft X-rays are confined to a thin, highly corrugated cold-hot interface (corrugation factor $\sim10$), whereas thermal emission fills the hot phase. Turbulent transport sustains high-charge ions at $T\sim 10^4$-$10^5$ K, where they encounter neutral donors. The low-temperature O VIII fraction exceeds that in a uniformly cooling isobaric parcel, demonstrating the importance of mixing to the ionization history. CX depletes this cool ion population, while continued entrainment maintains the supply. Including a metagalactic ionizing background changes the ion distribution and enhances CX surface brightness by a factor of a few in our CGM comparison, but preserves the cool origin of most CX emission. In the limit of sufficient neutral column, CX surface brightness is ion-supply limited: higher donor density increases local emissivity but shortens the reaction layer. The system-wide CX-to-thermal soft X-ray ratio also depends on the volume-to-interface scale $V/A_{\rm int}$, making CX a potential probe of multiphase structure in the CGM, galactic winds, and the GC.
